## Abstract

Programs that assign services to students scoring below an eligibility threshold are often evaluated with regression discontinuity designs. These estimates are internally valid but apply only to students at the margin of eligibility, who are rarely the students furthest behind. We use a two-year panel of Renaissance Star reading and mathematics scores from a large urban district to carry a causal estimate from the cutoff to the full population assigned to Targeted Skills Instruction (TSI), a virtual tutoring program integrated with Edmentum's Exact Path platform. We estimate the intent-to-treat effect of assignment four times, changing one element of the design at each step: a sharp regression discontinuity in endline levels; a difference-in-discontinuities that removes a pre-existing baseline gap; a two-period inverse probability-weighted difference-in-differences for all assigned students; and its six-period event-study extension. An exact algebraic equivalence joins the second and third estimates, so moving from the cutoff to the full population changes the sample, not the estimator. In reading, the effect rises from 0.11 standard deviations at the cutoff to 0.18 under the aligned near-cutoff estimator and 0.25 for the full assigned population. In mathematics, the cutoff benchmark is null once the baseline gap is removed, and the negative full-population estimates rely on one identification strategy and attenuate under alternative weighting. We read the mathematics evidence as ruling out benefit rather than demonstrating harm.
